## Abstract

KV cache growth is a major bottleneck for long-context inference in large language models. Existing methods are often dominated by binary eviction or representation approximation, which may underutilize tokens that are not critical for exact retention but are still reconstructable. We present VECTOR, a plug-and-play augmentation for eviction-based pipelines that introduces three-way token routing: retention, approximation, and eviction. VECTOR combines an importance signal from the base scorer with a reconstructability signal from an offline-calibrated regression-based value estimation. By leveraging reconstructability, VECTOR recovers useful value information that would otherwise be irreversibly lost under binary eviction, while preserving key vectors for attention routing stability. On LongBench, RULER with contexts up to 128K tokens, and multi-turn SCBench, VECTOR yields significant gains over its base eviction methods under high compression. At a 90% compression ratio, SnapKV augmented with VECTOR outperforms six competing compression methods, including D2O and RocketKV, on all three evaluated models. Since VECTOR makes all routing decisions at prefill, decoding runs on a standard compressed cache with no measurable overhead.

## 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) increasingly rely on long-context inference (Grattafiori et al., 2024; Team et al., 2024; Singh et al., 2025), yet their key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with sequence length and quickly becomes the dominant memory cost (Kwon et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023). This bottleneck limits practical deployment in many applications such as retrieval-heavy QA (Lewis et al., 2020), agent workflows (Yao et al., 2022), and multi-turn reasoning (Packer et al., 2023; Li et al., 2025b), where context windows are long and memory budgets are strict. As a result, KV cache compression has become a central system problem for long-context LLM serving (Kwon et al., 2023).

Existing KV compression methods mainly follow two strategies. The first strategy is importance-based eviction, where tokens are scored and low-score entries are permanently evicted (e.g., SnapKV (Li et al., 2024), KeyDiff (Park et al., 2025), KVzip (Kim et al., 2025)). While these methods are simple and efficient, their decision is inherently binary: tokens are either fully retained or completely discarded. Under tight budgets, such an irreversible eviction can substantially degrade downstream performance. Recent methods move beyond this binary decision along two axes. D2O (Wan et al., 2024) works on the token axis with retain, merge, and evict decisions, while ARKV (Lei and Ilager, 2026) works on the precision axis with full-precision, quantized, and evicted states.

The second strategy is representation approximation, which compresses KV representations through quantization, projection, or reconstruction (e.g., AQUA-KV (Shutova et al., 2025), EliteKV (Zhou et al., 2025), DeltaKV (Hao et al., 2026), Attention Matching (Zweiger et al., 2026)). Rather than removing tokens outright, these methods attempt to preserve information approximately after compression. However, many existing approaches require architectural modifications, retraining, or expensive online computation, such as retrieval-based reconstruction (Hao et al., 2026), context-dependent fitting (Zweiger et al., 2026), or model uptraining (Zhou et al., 2025).

To better balance memory reduction and downstream performance, we treat KV compression as a unified retain–approximate–evict allocation problem, where tokens are selectively retained, approximately reconstructed, or removed under a fixed memory budget. This perspective is motivated by two observations. First, recent non-binary methods (Lei and Ilager, 2026; Wan et al., 2024) demonstrate that going beyond binary eviction improves performance. However, their allocation decisions are driven by token importance signals such as attention scores or attention statistics. They do not explicitly model reconstructability, namely, whether a token’s KV representation can be accurately recovered from other available information with limited error. This distinction matters because not all important tokens are equally compressible: some can be safely approximated, while others are highly error-sensitive and should instead be retained exactly. Second, prior work on KV quantization suggests that keys and values exhibit asymmetric sensitivity to compression error, with values generally being more tolerant to approximation than keys (Liu et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2025a). However, existing token-level KV compression methods rarely exploit this asymmetry explicitly when allocating memory across tokens. This leaves room to improve both performance and compression efficiency.

Motivated by these observations, we raise two research questions. The first concerns the approximation mechanism; the second concerns the allocation strategy.

- • RQ1: Can we build a lightweight reconstruction mechanism that recovers value representations with low runtime overhead and no architectural retraining?

- • RQ2: Under a fixed KV memory budget, how should we jointly use importance and reconstructability to allocate tokens into retention, approximation, and eviction tiers?

To answer these questions, we propose VECTOR (Value Estimation via Collinearity and Three-way Orthogonal Routing), a plug-and-play augmentation for token-importance-based eviction methods. Unlike D2O (Wan et al., 2024), a standalone token-level pipeline driven by importance signals alone, VECTOR augments existing eviction backbones by introducing reconstructability as a second allocation dimension. VECTOR acts on the token axis, so it is orthogonal to precision-level methods such as ARKV (Lei and Ilager, 2026).

*Figure 1: Overview of VECTOR’s three-way token allocation. The base importance scorer first filters out unimportant tokens for eviction. For important tokens, VECTOR evaluates OLS-based $K\!\to\!V$ reconstruction error: tokens with small error enter Approximation, while tokens with large error remain in Retention. Approximation is applied to values only (V-only), with keys retained.*

For RQ1, VECTOR reconstructs values from keys with an offline-calibrated Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) map. Keys and values are linear projections of the same hidden state, which makes linear prediction feasible. VECTOR keeps keys exactly because they determine the softmax weights, where errors are amplified, while values are aggregated linearly and tolerate approximation (Liu et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2025a).

For RQ2, VECTOR allocates tokens along two orthogonal axes: importance from the base eviction method, and reconstructability from the OLS reconstruction error. Low-importance tokens are evicted. Among the rest, easy-to-reconstruct tokens are approximated, and the others are retained exactly. Under the same memory budget, this recovers information that binary eviction would discard.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

- • A reconstructability-aware allocation view of KV compression. As in Figure 1, we formulate KV budget allocation as a three-way token allocation problem that jointly considers importance and reconstructability, rather than a binary retention/eviction decision.

- • A lightweight K $\rightarrow$ V reconstruction module. We develop a one-time offline OLS calibration that enables online value reconstruction from the stored keys, with low inference-time overhead.

- • A plug-and-play upgrade for eviction baselines. VECTOR can be attached to representative token-importance eviction methods (e.g., attention-score-based and key-geometry-based) with minimal integration adaptations.

- • Empirical gains under strict memory budgets. On LongBench, RULER with up to 128K tokens, and multi-turn SCBench, adding VECTOR to eviction baselines yields significant gains under high compression. At $p_{c}=0.90$ , SnapKV+VECTOR outperforms six competing compression methods on all three evaluated models, and VECTOR adds no measurable decoding overhead.

## 2 Related Work

#### KV Cache Compression

Existing methods fall into three families. Eviction-based methods score tokens by importance and permanently discard low-scoring entries (Zhang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024; Park et al., 2025; Cai et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2025; Oren et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025). They are effective but operate as binary keep-or-drop policies, causing irreversible information loss under tight budgets. Quantization methods reduce bit-width across all cached entries (Liu et al., 2024b; Kang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025a; Shutova et al., 2025). They are less destructive but bounded in compression ratio and often require hardware support. Approximation methods reconstruct KV representations through low-rank projection or residual modeling (Chang et al., 2025; Hao et al., 2026; Zweiger et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2025). Non-binary allocation is also increasingly common, along two distinct axes. On the token axis, D2O uses retain, merge, and evict decisions (Wan et al., 2024). On the precision axis, ARKV assigns full-precision, quantized, and evicted states (Lei and Ilager, 2026). Another line keeps a larger KV pool and selects tokens dynamically during decoding, through sparse attention (Behnam et al., 2025) or CPU offloading (Sun et al., 2025).

#### Exploiting K–V Subspace Redundancy

Since K and V are both projected from the same hidden state, their shared structure can be exploited for compression. MLA compresses token memory into a shared latent representation (Liu et al., 2024a). AQUA-KV and EliteKV leverage K/V dependency through residual quantization and joint low-rank projection, respectively (Shutova et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025). These works support the view that the shared structure of K and V is a practically exploitable property.

#### Relation to Our Method

VECTOR is a plug-and-play augmentation for eviction-based pipelines, not a standalone compression method. Unlike approximation-oriented approaches (Chang et al., 2025; Hao et al., 2026), it requires no architectural modification or retraining and preserves full compatibility with existing eviction backbones. Within the eviction family, VECTOR extends binary retain/evict decisions by introducing a third approximation tier driven by reconstructability, a dimension that prior non-binary methods (Lei and Ilager, 2026; Wan et al., 2024) do not explicitly model. Because VECTOR acts on the token axis, it is orthogonal to precision-based compression. We therefore evaluate VECTOR as an augmentation over eviction baselines, which directly reflects its intended use case, and further compare it with six competing compression methods (Section 4.3).

## 3 Method

VECTOR extends token-importance-based eviction methods by introducing a third allocation state: approximation. As in Figure 1, token routing proceeds along two dimensions. The first is importance, provided by a base eviction scorer. The second is reconstructability, which measures how accurately a token’s value can be recovered from its key via a lightweight linear predictor. Together, these two dimensions determine whether each token is retained exactly, approximated, or evicted.

### 3.1 Approximation: Value Estimation via K–V Collinearity

While the above discussion motivates the incorporation of reconstructability into KV cache compression, it is crucial to recognize that keys and values exhibit different tolerances to approximation errors. Recent studies (Li et al., 2025a; Patel, 2026) have shown that even small perturbations in key vectors are exponentially amplified by the softmax function, leading to catastrophic disruptions in the attention probability distribution. In contrast, errors in value vectors propagate only linearly through the weighted sum, as values are applied after the softmax normalization. This asymmetry suggests that approximating keys is significantly more risky than approximating values.

Building on this observation, we adopt a $V$ -only estimation strategy for tokens in the Approximation state. Specifically, we retain the exact key vector to preserve the integrity of the attention routing mechanism, while discarding the original value vector to reclaim memory. The missing value is subsequently reconstructed using an alternative compact representation. This asymmetric treatment ensures that the critical attention map remains uncompromised while maximizing memory savings. We empirically validate this design choice in Appendix F, where K-only approximation shows inconsistent gains and occasionally degrades below the unaugmented baseline under medium-to-high compression, while V-only approximation consistently improves over it.

#### Empirical Evidence

Before presenting the full method design, we first verify a prerequisite of our approach: whether a simple linear map can reliably predict $V$ from $K$ across different model families, scales, and architectures. We employ the C4 dataset Dodge et al. (2021), a large-scale pre-training corpus, to collect key and value activation vectors at each transformer layer, drawing from 10,000 sequences of 4,096 tokens. For each layer, a linear model predicting $V$ from $K$ is subsequently fitted via OLS regression. To evaluate generalization, we additionally construct a held-out test set consisting of 100 sequences of 4,096 tokens, and report the mean $R^{2}$ of the OLS averaged across all layers within each model on this test set. As shown in Table 1, offline OLS achieves high $K\rightarrow V$ predictability on all tested models, with $R^{2}_{\textrm{global}}$ ranging from $0.6863$ to $0.9392$ . This result serves as the empirical foundation of our approximation strategy.

#### Remark

In standard attention, both $K\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}}$ and $V\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}}$ are linear projections of the same hidden state $h\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , i.e., $K=W_{K}h$ and $V=W_{V}h$ .11 1 Throughout this paper, we denote all vectors as column vectors, and linear transformations are written as $y=Wx$ . Exact reconstruction of $V$ from $K$ is impossible in general, since modern architectures use $d_{k},d_{v}\ll d$ (Vaswani et al., 2017; Shazeer, 2019; Ainslie et al., 2023; Grattafiori et al., 2024). However, the variance of $h$ is dominated by a low effective rank (Sun et al., 2024), and Multi-Head Latent Attention (Liu et al., 2024a) shows that $K$ and $V$ can share a low-dimensional latent representation. Both $K$ and $V$ are therefore well approximated by projections of a shared low-dimensional subspace, which makes predicting $V$ from $K$ feasible.

#### Why Not the Pseudo-Inverse?

Since $K=W_{K}h$ and $V=W_{V}h$ , a calibration-free alternative is $\hat{V}=W_{V}W_{\mathrm{MP}}K$ , where $W_{\mathrm{MP}}=W_{K}^{\top}(W_{K}W_{K}^{\top})^{-1}$ is the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse of $W_{K}$ . This estimator picks the minimum-norm $h^{\prime}$ consistent with $K$ , which is not chosen to predict $V$ well. In practice, it gives negative $R^{2}$ on most layers of four of the five models in Table 1, while OLS reaches 0.69 to 0.94 (Appendix E). We therefore fit $W_{\mathrm{OLS}}=\arg\min_{W}\mathbb{E}_{h\sim\mathcal{D}}\|WK-V\|_{2}^{2}$ to minimize the $V$ -prediction error directly, where $\mathcal{D}$ is the distribution of hidden states on a pre-training corpus. The calibration is also cheap. On Llama-3.1-8B, calibrating on $10\times$ fewer sequences (500) or on a different corpus does not significantly change downstream results (Appendix M).

#### RoPE Decoupling

A critical engineering challenge arises with Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) (Su et al., 2024), which is ubiquitously adopted in modern LLMs. RoPE applies a position-dependent rotation to the keys ( $K_{\textrm{post-RoPE}}=R_{m}W_{K}h$ at position $m$ ), while values remain position-independent ( $V=W_{V}h$ ). Fitting a static OLS matrix directly on post-RoPE keys would necessitate position-dependent estimators due to the entanglement of positional information, adding unnecessary complexity. To expose the intrinsic K-V collinearity, we explicitly decouple the positional information by applying an inexpensive inverse rotation ( $R_{m}^{-1}K_{\textrm{post-RoPE}}$ ) to the cached keys during the approximation phase. This lightweight decoupling allows the static $W_{\textrm{OLS}}$ to accurately reconstruct $V$ regardless of token position.

### 3.2 The VECTOR Pipeline

*Figure 2: Asymmetric three-way allocation: K is retained exactly for the expanded candidate pool, while V is split into Retain, Approximate, and Evict.*

In the following, we introduce the complete VECTOR pipeline for the three-way allocation. The pipeline is designed as a lightweight, plug-and-play extension that augments existing token-importance-based eviction algorithms (e.g., SnapKV (Li et al., 2024), KVzip (Kim et al., 2025), KeyDiff Park et al. (2025)).

Denote $p_{c}$ as the target memory compression ratio. To incorporate the Approximation state while preserving the same memory budget, VECTOR executes the following three-step pipeline:

Step 1: Budget Relaxation. Let $p_{a}$ denote the approximation ratio. VECTOR invokes the base token-importance eviction algorithm to identify an expanded candidate pool of size $1-p_{c}+p_{a}$ . This yields a larger initial set of contextually relevant tokens, from which we subsequently determine which ones to compress.

Step 2: Residual Evaluation. For each token in the expanded candidate pool, VECTOR computes the per-token reconstruction error $\varepsilon_{i}=\|V_{i}-W_{\textrm{OLS}}K_{i}\|^{2}_{2}$ using the offline-calibrated OLS projection matrix $W_{\textrm{OLS}}$ . This step introduces an orthogonal dimension of evaluation—reconstructability—that quantifies the approximation error incurred if the token’s value were discarded.

Step 3: Asymmetric Truncation. As illustrated in Figure 2, VECTOR partitions the expanded pool based on the computed reconstruction errors to execute the budget swap:

- • The keys of all $1-p_{c}+p_{a}$ tokens in the expanded pool are retained.

- • The $2p_{a}$ tokens with the lowest reconstruction errors $\varepsilon_{i}$ (i.e., those most amenable to approximation) have their cached values discarded. Their values are reconstructed from the retained keys as $\hat{V}=W_{\textrm{OLS}}K$ .

- • Both keys and values are exactly retained for the remaining $1-p_{c}-p_{a}$ proportion of tokens.

Through the above procedure, $1-p_{c}+p_{a}$ keys and $1-p_{c}-p_{a}$ values are stored in memory, consuming the exact same footprint as $1-p_{c}$ full KV pairs. Specifically, the Eviction, Approximation, and Retention states account for proportions $p_{c}-p_{a}$ , $2p_{a}$ , and $1-p_{c}-p_{a}$ of all tokens, respectively.

#### Memory Budget

The compression ratio $p_{c}$ fixes the total memory budget, and $p_{a}$ only decides how this budget is spent. Retaining a token costs a key and a value, approximating it costs only a key, and evicting it costs nothing. Increasing $p_{a}$ by $\delta$ moves $\delta$ tokens from retention and $\delta$ tokens from eviction into approximation, so the total memory stays unchanged. As a result, VECTOR supports any compression ratio that the base eviction method supports, and setting $p_{a}=0$ recovers the base method. Under the same budget, the approximation tier lets $1-p_{c}+p_{a}$ tokens keep their keys instead of $1-p_{c}$ . As in the base eviction methods, all routing decisions are made once at the end of prefill (Appendix H).

#### When Does Approximation Help?

Let $w_{i}$ be the importance score of token $i$ , normalized to sum to one. We measure the distortion after compression by $\mathcal{E}$ , the importance-weighted signal loss. An evicted token contributes $w_{i}$ , a retained token contributes $0$ , and an approximated token contributes $w_{i}$ times its normalized reconstruction error $\|V_{i}-\hat{V}_{i}\|_{2}^{2}/\|V_{i}\|_{2}^{2}$ . Let $R^{2}_{\textrm{approx}}$ be the OLS prediction quality over the approximated tokens, $w^{*}$ the importance score at the eviction boundary, and $\bar{w}$ the average importance score in the expanded pool.

#### Proposition 1.

Assume that the per-token reconstruction errors are independent of the importance scores, and that $p_{a}$ is small. Increasing $p_{a}$ reduces $\mathcal{E}$ if

$$ R^{2}_{\textrm{approx}}>\frac{\bar{w}}{w^{*}+\bar{w}}. $$

The proof is given in Appendix C.1. The approximation tier therefore helps most when the evicted tokens still carry substantial importance, that is, when $w^{*}$ is large relative to $\bar{w}$ .

#### Choice of $p_{a}$

Since $w^{*}$ and $\bar{w}$ vary across samples, we set $p_{a}$ with a fixed rule instead of tuning it per sample:

$$ p_{a}^{\mathrm{deploy}}=\min\!\left(p_{c}/2,\;(1-p_{c}-\epsilon)/2\right), $$

where $\epsilon>0$ is a small constant ensuring a non-empty Retention tier. The first term keeps the Approximation tier no larger than half the compressed budget, and the second ensures sufficient headroom for the Retention tier. A sensitivity analysis of $p_{a}$ is given in Section 4.7.

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

We conduct all experiments with the KVPress evaluation framework (Devoto et al., 2025) under a unified protocol for long-context compression.

Before downstream evaluation, VECTOR performs a one-time offline calibration to fit the layer-wise linear map $W_{\mathrm{OLS}}$ used for value reconstruction. Following the protocol in Section 3.1, we use C4 dataset (Dodge et al., 2021) to collect key–value activation pairs from 5,000 sequences (Llama-3.1-8B) or 10,000 sequences (Qwen3 models) of 2,048 tokens, and fit OLS per transformer layer. The resulting calibrated weights are then fixed for all downstream experiments.

#### Baselines

We evaluate four representative token-eviction baselines and their VECTOR-augmented variants: KeyDiff (Park et al., 2025), SnapKV (Li et al., 2024), KVzip (Kim et al., 2025), and PyramidKV (Cai et al., 2024). These methods differ in how they score token importance. Query-aware methods (SnapKV, PyramidKV) identify important tokens via the attention patterns that the query induces over the context, producing task-relevant eviction decisions that are tailored to the specific question being asked. Query-agnostic methods (KeyDiff, KVzip) score tokens using properties intrinsic to the context itself (i.e., key geometric diversity for KeyDiff and semantic redundancy for KVzip) without access to the query. For each baseline, the corresponding “+ VECTOR” variant retains the original importance scorer and augments it with the reconstructability-aware approximation tier.

#### Competing Methods

We further compare with six compression methods: ChunkKV (Liu et al., 2025), ExpectedAttention (Devoto et al., 2025), AdaKV-SnapKV (Feng et al., 2024), TOVA (Oren et al., 2024), D2O (Wan et al., 2024), and RocketKV (Behnam et al., 2025). All methods use the same prompts, scorer, and compression ratios as the main experiments. Protocol details are given in Appendix G.

#### Models

We report results on three open-source models: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Qwen3-14B (Yang et al., 2025), and Qwen3-0.6B (Yang et al., 2025).

#### Benchmarks

We use LongBench (Bai et al., 2024) as the primary quantitative benchmark and Needle-in-a-Haystack (NIAH) (Kamradt, 2023) as a stress test for long-range retrieval (Appendix J). For LongBench, we evaluate on a 16-task subset obtained by excluding the 5 Chinese-language tasks from the original 21-task collection, using the full test split. We further evaluate long-context retrieval with RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024) at context lengths from 16K to 128K tokens, and multi-turn reuse of a compressed cache with SCBench (Li et al., 2025b) in Appendix K.

#### Metrics

LongBench tasks are evaluated with their official task-specific metrics (F1, ROUGE-L, exact match / accuracy, and edit similarity); we report Avg as the arithmetic mean over the 16 selected tasks. We evaluate compression ratios $p_{c}\in\{0.25,0.50,0.75,0.90\}$ , with the corresponding approximation ratios set by Eq. (1): $p_{a}\in\{0.125,0.25,0.125,0.05\}$ , respectively. Since greedy decoding is deterministic, we quantify uncertainty with a paired bootstrap over test samples (Koehn, 2004) with 10,000 resamples (Appendix L).

More implementation and reproducibility details are provided in Appendix D.

### 4.2 LongBench Main Results

Table 2 reports the LongBench results. Augmenting eviction baselines with VECTOR improves downstream performance under high compression, where binary eviction discards the most information. At $p_{c}=0.90$ , VECTOR improves 10 of the 12 base methods across the three models.

The strongest and most consistent improvements are observed with the two query-agnostic baselines, KeyDiff and KVzip. For KeyDiff, gains are particularly pronounced at high compression: on Qwen3-14B, KeyDiff+VECTOR improves the average score by $+7.03$ points at $p_{c}{=}0.50$ , $+9.15$ at $p_{c}{=}0.75$ , and $+9.73$ at $p_{c}{=}0.90$ . Similar gains are observed on Qwen3-0.6B (Table 2). On Llama-3.1-8B, the gains of KeyDiff+VECTOR are significant at both $p_{c}=0.75$ and $p_{c}=0.90$ (Appendix L). KVzip+VECTOR improves over KVzip at $p_{c}=0.90$ on all three models, by $+3.97$ , $+2.78$ , and $+2.77$ points on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-14B, and Qwen3-0.6B. These results support the central claim of this work: introducing a reconstructability-aware approximation tier can recover a substantial portion of the information that would otherwise be irretrievably lost under binary eviction.

For the query-aware baselines, VECTOR is most effective at the highest compression ratio. At $p_{c}=0.90$ , SnapKV+VECTOR improves over SnapKV on all three models, by $+1.82$ , $+1.36$ , and $+1.63$ points, and the gain on Llama-3.1-8B is significant (95% CI $[+1.06,+2.54]$ ). As shown in Section 3.2, the approximation tier helps most when the evicted tokens still carry substantial importance. This holds under high compression, and also with query-agnostic scorers, which select tokens without seeing the question.

### 4.5 Reconstructability Signal

VECTOR selects the approximated tokens by reconstruction error. To test whether this signal matters, we keep the candidate pool and the budget fixed, and replace the selection rule with importance ranking, which approximates the least important candidates. We use KeyDiff+VECTOR on Llama-3.1-8B with six LongBench QA tasks at $p_{c}\in\{0.75,0.90\}$ (Appendix D.4). Selecting by reconstruction error outperforms selecting by importance by 2.31 points on average, and wins in 10 of the 12 settings. The correlation between importance and reconstruction error is only 0.16. The two signals are nearly independent, so importance cannot replace the reconstruction error when choosing which tokens to approximate.

### 4.6 Inference Overhead

We measure decoding throughput and prefill time at a 32K context and $p_{c}=0.90$ , for KeyDiff, SnapKV, and PyramidKV on all three models (Appendix H). In all nine settings, VECTOR and its base method have the same decoding throughput within measurement noise, because both decode with standard attention over a compressed cache. Value reconstruction adds a one-time prefill cost of 0.16 to 0.21 seconds, which is 6% of the prefill time for Qwen3-14B and 9% for Llama-3.1-8B. The OLS matrices take 67 MB for Llama-3.1-8B, independent of context length and batch size.

## 5 Conclusion

We propose VECTOR, a lightweight three-way allocation framework that integrates reconstructability-aware approximation into existing eviction methods. By separating token importance from reconstructability, VECTOR extends binary retain/evict decisions into retention, approximation, and eviction under the same memory budget. Value approximation uses an offline OLS calibration without model retraining, and our analysis links the OLS $R^{2}$ to the reduction in distortion. Empirically, augmenting representative baselines with VECTOR yields significant gains under high compression on LongBench, RULER with up to 128K tokens, and multi-turn SCBench. At $p_{c}=0.90$ , the best VECTOR-augmented method outperforms six competing compression methods, and VECTOR adds no measurable decoding overhead. These results suggest that combining importance-aware eviction with reconstructability-aware approximation is a promising direction for long-context inference.

## Limitations

VECTOR has some limitations. First, $p_{a}$ is set by a fixed rule (Eq. (1)) that is shared by all base scorers, budgets, and layers. Adapting $p_{a}$ to the base scorer and the budget is a natural extension. For example, query-aware scorers at moderate budgets already retain most query-relevant tokens and may benefit from a smaller approximation tier (Appendix I). Second, our implementation is built on KVPress without custom kernels. A fused attention kernel that stores only keys for approximated tokens would realize the memory layout of Section 3.2 directly (Appendix H).

## Appendix B Theoretical Analysis

We analyze the effect of introducing the Approximation state under a fixed memory budget. The central question is: under what conditions does expanding the Approximation tier reduce information loss, compared to binary eviction?

To formalize this, we define $\mathcal{E}$ as an importance-weighted measure of signal loss after compression. Each token contributes its signal loss weighted by its importance score $w_{i}$ . The signal loss is $1$ for an evicted token, $0$ for a retained token, and the normalized reconstruction error ${\|V_{i}-\hat{V}_{i}\|_{2}^{2}}/{\|V_{i}\|_{2}^{2}}\in[0,1]$ for an approximated token. A smaller $\mathcal{E}$ means less distortion to the attention computation.

We then characterize when expanding the Approximation state reduces $\mathcal{E}$ (Proposition 1). The key quantity is $R^{2}_{\textrm{approx}}$ , the OLS prediction quality measured specifically over the tokens selected for approximation. Intuitively, $R^{2}_{\textrm{approx}}$ close to $1$ means approximated tokens are well-reconstructed, contributing little to $\mathcal{E}$ . We derive a threshold on $R^{2}_{\textrm{approx}}$ that depends on the skewness of the importance score distribution. We also provide a closed-form expression for $\mathcal{E}$ under a Gaussian residual assumption (Example 1).

Let $\mathcal{I}_{E}(p_{a},p_{c})$ and $\mathcal{I}_{A}(p_{a},p_{c})$ denote the index sets of evicted and approximated tokens, respectively, and let $w_{i}$ denote the importance score of the $i$ -th token. We then write $\mathcal{E}$ as:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}(p_{a},p_{c}) \displaystyle=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{E}(p_{a},p_{c})}w_{i} \displaystyle\quad+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{A}(p_{a},p_{c})}w_{i}\frac{\|V_{i}-\hat{V}_{i}\|_{2}^{2}}{\|V_{i}\|^{2}_{2}} \displaystyle\approx\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{E}(p_{a},p_{c})}w_{i}+\Bigl(\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{A}(p_{a},p_{c})}w_{i}\Bigr)\,\mu_{A}, $$

where the approximation assumes that the per-token reconstruction errors ${\|V_{i}-\hat{V}_{i}\|_{2}^{2}}/{\|V_{i}\|_{2}^{2}}$ are approximately independent of the importance scores $w_{i}$ , and $\mu_{A}=1-R^{2}_{\textrm{approx}}(p_{a},p_{c})$ denotes the mean relative reconstruction error over $\mathcal{I}_{A}$ . Here, $R^{2}_{\textrm{approx}}(p_{a},p_{c})$ is the $R^{2}$ computed solely over the tokens in the Approximation set.

Under this approximation, Proposition 1 (Section 3.2) gives the condition on $R^{2}_{\textrm{approx}}$ under which expanding the Approximation state reduces $\mathcal{E}$ . There, $\bar{w}=\left(1-\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{E}}w_{i}\right)/(1-p_{c}+p_{a})$ is the average importance score of the tokens in the expanded pool, and $w^{*}$ is the importance score of the token at the truncation boundary of the Eviction set. The proof is given in Appendix C.1.

Based on Proposition 1, the required predictability $R^{2}_{\textrm{approx}}$ is governed by the skewness of the importance score distribution. When expanding the Approximation tier, tokens enter from both the Eviction set (gaining recovery) and the Retention set (incurring approximation error). For highly skewed distributions where $\bar{w}\gg w^{*}$ , the latter effect dominates, and OLS must achieve higher accuracy to compensate and yield a net reduction in distortion.

Besides the above, the following example adopts a Gaussian assumption on the OLS residuals to examine how the shape of the residual distribution affects $R^{2}_{\textrm{approx}}$ and, consequently, $\mathcal{E}$ :

#### Example 1.

Let $\phi$ and $\Phi$ denote the PDF and CDF of the standard normal distribution, respectively. Let $r_{i}$ denote the signed OLS residual for the $i$ -th token, satisfying $r_{i}^{2}=\|V_{i}-\hat{V}_{i}\|_{2}^{2}=\varepsilon_{i}$ . Assume $r_{i}\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})$ , and let $\Sigma^{2}$ denote the variance of $\|V_{i}\|_{2}$ ( $\Sigma^{2}>\sigma^{2}$ ). Define $\eta(p_{a},p_{c}):=\sigma\,\Phi^{-1}\!\left(1/2+p_{a}/(1-p_{c}+p_{a})\right)$ . Then, given a target retention ratio $1-p_{c}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}(p_{a},p_{c}) \displaystyle\approx\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{E}(p_{a},p_{c})}w_{i} \displaystyle\quad+2p_{a}\bar{w}\,\bigl(1-R^{2}_{\textrm{approx}}(p_{a},p_{c})\bigr), $$

with

$$ 1-R^{2}_{\textrm{approx}}=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\Sigma^{2}}\Bigl(1-\tfrac{1-p_{c}+p_{a}}{p_{a}}\,\tfrac{\eta}{\sigma}\,\phi\bigl(\tfrac{\eta}{\sigma}\bigr)\Bigr), $$

where $\eta$ is short for $\eta(p_{a},p_{c})$ . This shows that $1-R^{2}_{\textrm{approx}}(p_{a},p_{c})$ depends on $\sigma^{2}$ and $\Sigma^{2}$ under the Gaussian distribution.

Combining Proposition 1 and Example 1, when the importance score distribution concentrates on the Approximation and Retention sets (i.e., $\bar{w}\gg w^{*}$ ), the method is effective provided that the values are highly predictable from the keys, i.e., $\sigma^{2}\ll\Sigma^{2}$ .

## Appendix C Proofs

### C.1 Proof of Proposition 1

Given the formula for $\mathcal{E}$ and $\mu_{A}$ , we have

$$ \mathcal{E}(p_{a},p_{c})\approx\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{E}(p_{a},p_{c})}w_{i}\\
+\Bigl(\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{A}(p_{a},p_{c})}w_{i}\Bigr)\bigl(1-R^{2}_{\textrm{approx}}(p_{a},p_{c})\bigr). $$

Since $w^{*}$ is the importance score at the truncation boundary, $\mathcal{I}_{E}$ has proportion $p_{c}-p_{a}$ , and $\mathcal{I}_{A}$ contains $2p_{a}$ proportion of tokens, we have

$$ \sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{E}(p_{a}+\delta,p_{c})}\!\!w_{i}-\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{E}(p_{a},p_{c})}\!\!w_{i}\approx-w^{*}\delta, $$

i.e., increasing $p_{a}$ by $\delta$ removes $\delta$ boundary tokens with weight $w^{*}$ from $\mathcal{I}_{E}$ . Similarly,

$$ \sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{A}(p_{a}+\delta,p_{c})}\!\!w_{i}-\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{A}(p_{a},p_{c})}\!\!w_{i}\approx(w^{*}+\bar{w})\delta, $$

since $|\mathcal{I}_{A}|$ grows by $2\delta$ : $\delta$ tokens enter from $\mathcal{I}_{E}$ with weight $w^{*}$ , and $\delta$ tokens enter from the Retention set with weight $\approx\bar{w}$ . The latter holds because the partition between Approximation and Retention is determined by reconstruction error rather than importance score, so the transferred tokens carry average weight $\bar{w}$ .

Combining the above, we obtain:

$$ \mathcal{E}(p_{a}+\delta,p_{c})-\mathcal{E}(p_{a},p_{c})\approx-w^{*}\delta\\
+(w^{*}+\bar{w})\delta\bigl(1-R^{2}_{\textrm{approx}}(p_{a},p_{c})\bigr)\\
-2p_{a}\bar{w}\delta\frac{\partial R^{2}_{\textrm{approx}}}{\partial p_{a}}. $$

For $\mathcal{E}(p_{a}+\delta,p_{c})<\mathcal{E}(p_{a},p_{c})$ (with $\delta>0$ ), we require (writing $D:=2p_{a}\bar{w}\,\partial R^{2}_{\textrm{approx}}/\partial p_{a}$ for brevity):

$$ \displaystyle-w^{*}+(w^{*}+\bar{w})\bigl(1-R^{2}_{\textrm{approx}}\bigr)-D<0 \displaystyle\Leftrightarrow\; \displaystyle(w^{*}+\bar{w})\bigl(1-R^{2}_{\textrm{approx}}\bigr)<w^{*}+D \displaystyle\Leftrightarrow\; \displaystyle 1-R^{2}_{\textrm{approx}}<\frac{w^{*}+D}{w^{*}+\bar{w}} \displaystyle\Leftrightarrow\; \displaystyle R^{2}_{\textrm{approx}}>1-\frac{w^{*}+D}{w^{*}+\bar{w}}. $$

For small $p_{a}$ , the term $D$ is negligible, yielding:

$$ R^{2}_{\textrm{approx}}(p_{a},p_{c})>1-\frac{w^{*}}{w^{*}+\bar{w}}=\frac{\bar{w}}{w^{*}+\bar{w}}.\qed $$

### C.2 Proof of Example 1

Since the selection of $\mathcal{I}_{E}(p_{a},p_{c})$ is independent of the reconstruction error, the signed residuals $r_{i}$ of non-evicted tokens follow the same $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})$ distribution. Further invoking the independence between $r_{i}^{2}$ and $w_{i}$ , the overall distortion is:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}(p_{a},p_{c}) \displaystyle=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{E}(p_{a},p_{c})}w_{i}+\frac{1}{\Sigma^{2}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{A}(p_{a},p_{c})}w_{i}r_{i}^{2} \displaystyle\approx\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{E}(p_{a},p_{c})}w_{i} \displaystyle\quad+\frac{2p_{a}\bar{w}}{\Sigma^{2}}\cdot\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{A}(p_{a},p_{c})}r_{i}^{2}}{|\mathcal{I}_{A}(p_{a},p_{c})|}. $$

Since the Approximation set selects the $2p_{a}$ tokens with the smallest reconstruction errors (i.e., those with $|r_{i}|\leq\eta(p_{a},p_{c})$ ), corresponding to the central $2p_{a}/(1-p_{c}+p_{a})$ fraction of the Gaussian distribution, the conditional distribution of $r_{i}$ given $i\in\mathcal{I}_{A}(p_{a},p_{c})$ is a truncated normal on $[-\eta(p_{a},p_{c}),\,\eta(p_{a},p_{c})]$ , where $\eta(p_{a},p_{c})=\sigma\Phi^{-1}(1/2+p_{a}/(1-p_{c}+p_{a}))$ , and $2\Phi(\eta/\sigma)-1=2p_{a}/(1-p_{c}+p_{a})$ .

Recalling that for $X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})$ :

$$ \mathbb{E}(X^{2}\mid|X|\leq x)=\sigma^{2}\!\left[1-\frac{2(x/\sigma)\phi(x/\sigma)}{2\Phi(x/\sigma)-1}\right], $$

we obtain, with $\eta$ short for $\eta(p_{a},p_{c})$ :

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}(p_{a},p_{c}) \displaystyle\approx\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{E}(p_{a},p_{c})}w_{i} \displaystyle\quad+2p_{a}\bar{w}\,\bigl(1-R^{2}_{\textrm{approx}}(p_{a},p_{c})\bigr), $$

where

$$ 1-R^{2}_{\textrm{approx}}=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\Sigma^{2}}\Bigl(1-\tfrac{1-p_{c}+p_{a}}{p_{a}}\,\tfrac{\eta}{\sigma}\,\phi\bigl(\tfrac{\eta}{\sigma}\bigr)\Bigr).\qed $$

## Appendix H Implementation and Efficiency Details

#### Prefill and decoding

VECTOR makes all routing decisions once at the end of prefill, as its base eviction methods do. The base scorer ranks the tokens, the reconstruction error is computed for the candidate pool, and each token is assigned to a tier. The reconstructed value $\hat{V}=W_{\mathrm{OLS}}K$ of an approximated token depends only on its retained key. Our implementation computes it in the same pass and writes it into the cache, so decoding is standard attention over the compressed cache. A kernel that stores only keys for approximated tokens can instead reconstruct their values during decoding, which gives the same values.

#### Memory accounting

Let $B=1-p_{c}$ , and let $C$ denote the memory of the keys (or values) of all tokens. Exactly retained tokens store a key and a value, and approximated tokens store only a key. VECTOR therefore stores $(B-p_{a})\cdot 2C+2p_{a}\cdot C=2BC$ , which equals the base eviction method. Our implementation is built on KVPress, which keeps keys and values in paired tensors of the same length, and we do not write a custom kernel. Approximated tokens are therefore stored with their reconstructed values, and the measured cache at $p_{c}=0.90$ is $1.5\times$ that of the base method (Table 12). A key-only layout for approximated tokens attains $2BC$ . The OLS matrices add $n_{\text{layers}}\times d_{kv}^{2}$ parameters, which is 67 MB in bf16 for Llama-3.1-8B, independent of context length and batch size.

#### Timing protocol

We measure on one NVIDIA H200 GPU with batch size 1 and PyTorch SDPA attention, using warm-up runs and CUDA synchronization. Decoding throughput is measured as the difference between a long and a short generation, which cancels the prefill cost. Each configuration is repeated five times, and Table 13 reports the mean and standard deviation. These measurements use a PyTorch implementation without custom kernels.

#### Prefill cost

Value reconstruction adds a nearly constant one-time cost at prefill. At 32K tokens, it is 0.21 s for Qwen3-14B, 0.18 s for Llama-3.1-8B, and 0.16 s for Qwen3-0.6B. Relative to the prefill time, this is 6% for Qwen3-14B and 9% for Llama-3.1-8B, and the share decreases as the context grows.

#### FlashAttention compatibility

VECTOR only rewrites the KV cache after prefill, so it does not depend on the attention kernel. We verified that VECTOR runs with FlashAttention-3 (Shah et al., 2024). On HotpotQA samples with SnapKV, KeyDiff, and PyramidKV at $p_{c}=0.90$ , 96% to 98.5% of the compressed cache entries are identical to the SDPA run, and the remaining differences come from bf16 rounding at the selection boundary. All reported numbers use PyTorch SDPA.

## Appendix J Needle-in-a-Haystack Results

To further assess retrieval robustness under strict memory budgets, we evaluate NIAH on Llama-3.1-8B across all four baselines and their VECTOR-augmented variants. We focus on the high-compression regime $p_{c}{=}0.90$ (with $p_{a}{=}0.05$ per Eq. (1)), where differences between methods are most pronounced. We use a $10{\times}10$ grid over context lengths $\{3\text{k},6\text{k},\ldots,30\text{k}\}$ and needle depths $\{0,11,22,\ldots,100\}\%$ ; each cell is averaged over 5 independent runs and reported as ROUGE-L F1. Figure 4 shows the resulting heatmaps.

Across all four baseline families, VECTOR consistently improves retrieval quality, though the magnitude of gain varies by baseline. The largest improvement is observed for KVzip, where the baseline exhibits broad low-score regions and KVzip+VECTOR substantially recovers performance across both context lengths and needle depths. For KeyDiff, VECTOR provides clear gains, primarily lifting low-score cells at harder depth–length combinations. For SnapKV and PyramidKV, whose baselines are already strong at this compression ratio, improvements are more moderate but consistently positive.

Overall, these results further support the role of reconstructability-aware approximation under tight memory budgets: rather than merely shifting average scores upward, VECTOR changes the failure pattern from large contiguous low-score regions to more localized difficult cells, indicating improved robustness under challenging retrieval conditions.
